tool.name: subprocess
tool.tagline: Run external programs from Python and talk to their input and output
tool.description: subprocess is the standard way to start other programs from Python, pass them arguments and input, capture their output and react to their exit status. It replaces os.system and shell scripts in build tools, deployment scripts, test harnesses and automation. Learning it well means scripts that are safe from shell injection, never hang, and fail loudly.

glossary.def: A program started by another running program (its parent). The parent can wait for the child, read its output and get its exit code.
An attack where text from outside (a file name, a form field) is pasted into a shell command and the shell runs part of it as an extra command of the attacker's choosing.
A short message the operating system sends to a running program, such as 'please stop' or 'the user pressed Ctrl+C'. The program can react to some signals; others end it at once.
End of file: the sign that there is no more data to read, because a file ended or the other side closed its end of a pipe or connection.
A finished child process whose parent hasn't yet waited for it; the operating system keeps an empty entry for it only so the parent can read its exit code.
A set of related processes on Linux or macOS, such as a program and everything it started, that can be sent a signal all at once.
On Linux and macOS, the set of processes tied to one terminal; they receive Ctrl+C from it and are told when it closes.
On Linux and macOS, making a new process by copying the running one: the copy starts with everything the original had in memory.
On Linux and macOS, the step that replaces the program running in a process with a different program, keeping the same process ID.
The object subprocess.run returns once a program has finished: it holds the command, the exit code (returncode) and any captured output.
subprocess's class for starting a program without waiting for it, so you can read its output live, send it input, or stop it.

concepts.name: Running a command with run()
concepts.summary: Start another program from Python with subprocess.run, passing the command as a list, and check whether it succeeded.
concepts.why: Almost every automation script needs to call another tool, such as git, a video converter or a program that builds software.
concepts.body:
You've typed commands in the terminal, like `python hello.py`. A command is a program's name followed by extra words telling it what to do; those words are its **command-line arguments**. The `subprocess` module lets your Python code run such commands itself.

A running program is called a **process**. When your script starts another program, the new one is its **child process** (the child), and your script is the parent.

`subprocess.run(args)` starts a program, waits for it to finish, and returns a `CompletedProcess` object describing what happened. Pass the command as a **list**: the program name first, then each argument as its own element.

```python
subprocess.run(["git", "status", "--short"])
```

Each list element reaches the program exactly as written. Nothing in between reinterprets it, so spaces, quotes and `$` signs inside an argument need no special treatment. The program itself is found by searching the folders listed in **PATH**, a setting that tells the system where programs live.

The result has:

- `returncode`: the program's **exit code**, the number it reports when it ends. 0 means success; anything else means some kind of failure.
- `args`: what you ran.
- `stdout` / `stderr`: `None` unless you asked to capture the output (next lesson).

By default the child shares your terminal, so its output appears directly on screen, and `run` waits until it ends.

`run` is the recommended function and covers most needs. Older functions such as `call`, `check_call` and `check_output` still exist and are thin wrappers around it. Avoid `os.system` in new code: it always hands your command, as one string, to the **shell** (the program in a terminal that reads typed commands; see the shell=True lesson), and its result is harder to read.

To run another Python script in a way that works on every computer, use `sys.executable` (the full path, from the top of the disk, of the Python running your script) as the program instead of `"python"`.
concepts.code:
import subprocess, sys

r = subprocess.run(["echo", "hello", "world with spaces"])   # echo prints its arguments
# hello world with spaces
print(r.returncode)          # 0
print(r.args)                # ['echo', 'hello', 'world with spaces']

# -c runs the Python code given as text; sys.exit(3) ends with exit code 3
r = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", "import sys; sys.exit(3)"])
print(r.returncode)          # 3
print(r.stdout)              # None (not captured)
takeaways: run() starts a program, waits, and returns a CompletedProcess
Pass the command as a list of separate arguments
An exit code (returncode) of 0 means success
pitfalls: Passing one string like 'ls -l' without shell=True; on Linux and macOS it looks for a program literally named 'ls -l'.

quiz.q: What does subprocess.run(['ls', '-l', 'my file']) pass to ls (the file-listing program)?
options: One string 'ls -l my file' to the shell
It raises because of the space
quiz.explain: Each list element is passed as exactly one argument, spaces included.

concepts.name: Capturing output
concepts.summary: Capture what a command prints, as text, with capture_output=True and text=True.
concepts.why: Most scripts need to use what a command prints, such as a version number or a list of files.
concepts.body:
A program has two separate output channels. Normal results go to **standard output** (stdout). Error messages go to **standard error** (stderr), so they stay visible even when normal output is saved somewhere else. In a terminal, both appear on screen.

To get the output into Python instead, pass `capture_output=True`. Then `result.stdout` and `result.stderr` hold what the program wrote.

By default they are `bytes`. Add `text=True` to turn them into `str` using your computer's default encoding (normally UTF-8), or pass `encoding="utf-8"` to be explicit, which also gives you `str`. `text=True` also turns Windows line endings (`\r\n`) into `\n`.

```python
out = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "--version"],
                     capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip()
```

Remember `.strip()`: command output usually ends with a newline.

Finer control comes from the `stdout=` and `stderr=` parameters:

- `subprocess.PIPE`: capture it. A **pipe** is a one-way channel: the program writes into one end and Python reads from the other (`capture_output` sets this for both).
- `subprocess.DEVNULL`: throw it away.
- `stderr=subprocess.STDOUT`: send error messages into stdout, keeping them in order with the rest.
- An open file object: write straight into that file.

You can't combine `capture_output=True` with `stdout=` or `stderr=`. Captured output is kept in memory until the program ends. That's fine for normal commands, but not for one that prints huge amounts; read such output bit by bit with `Popen` (a later lesson).
concepts.code:
import subprocess, sys

code = "import sys; print('to out'); print('to err', file=sys.stderr)"
r = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", code], capture_output=True)
print(r.stdout)                         # b'to out\n'

r = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", code], capture_output=True, text=True)
print(repr(r.stdout), repr(r.stderr))   # 'to out\n' 'to err\n'

r = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", code], text=True,
                   stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT)
print(r.stdout.splitlines())            # ['to out', 'to err']

subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", code], stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL,
               stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)  # prints nothing
takeaways: capture_output=True fills result.stdout and result.stderr
text=True (or encoding=) gives str instead of bytes
PIPE, DEVNULL, STDOUT and file objects decide where each output goes
pitfalls: Forgetting text=True and then comparing bytes output with a str.

quiz.q: Which call merges a command's errors into result.stdout?
quiz.explain: stderr=STDOUT sends the error output into the captured stdout.

concepts.name: Failing loudly with check=True
concepts.summary: Turn non-zero exit codes into exceptions with check=True and handle CalledProcessError and FileNotFoundError.
concepts.why: Scripts that ignore failed commands carry on with broken results; exceptions stop them where the problem is.
concepts.body:
`run` does **not** raise an exception when a command fails: a non-zero `returncode` is just a number on the result, and it's easy to forget to check it. Pass `check=True`, and a non-zero exit code raises `subprocess.CalledProcessError`. It carries `returncode`, `cmd`, and the captured `stdout` / `stderr` (if you captured them).

```python
try:
    # make test: run a project's tests with the make tool
    subprocess.run(["make", "test"], check=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
    print(e.returncode, e.stderr)
```

Use `check=True` by default in scripts. Leave it off only when a non-zero code is an expected answer. For example, `grep` (which searches text) returns 1 for "no match", and `diff` (which compares files) returns 1 for "files differ". Then look at `returncode` yourself, or call `result.check_returncode()` later.

A different failure happens before the program even runs. If the program doesn't exist, you get `FileNotFoundError`; if the file isn't allowed to run as a program, `PermissionError`. Both are kinds of `OSError`. `shutil.which("git")` lets you check for a tool up front and print a friendly message.

`CalledProcessError` and `TimeoutExpired` (a later lesson) both count as `subprocess.SubprocessError`, so one `except subprocess.SubprocessError:` catches either.
takeaways: run() never raises on a non-zero exit code unless check=True
CalledProcessError carries returncode, stdout and stderr
A missing program raises FileNotFoundError before anything runs
pitfalls: Running a build step without check=True and continuing after it failed.

quiz.q: subprocess.run(['false']) is called without check (false is a program that just exits with code 1). What happens?
options: It returns a CompletedProcess with returncode 1
quiz.explain: Without check=True, failure is only visible in returncode.

concepts.name: shell=True and safe quoting
concepts.summary: Know what shell=True does, why it lets attackers run their own commands, and how shlex.quote and shlex.split help.
concepts.why: Letting outside text slip into a shell command is one of the most common security bugs in scripts.
concepts.body:
A **shell** is the program inside your terminal that reads the commands you type and runs them; Bash and PowerShell are shells. It understands extra symbols: `|` sends one program's output into another (a **pipe**), `>` saves output to a file, `*.txt` means every .txt file, `&&` runs a second command only if the first succeeds, and `$NAME` inserts a setting's value.

With `shell=True`, you pass a **single string**, and Python hands it to a shell (`/bin/sh` on Linux and macOS, `cmd.exe` on Windows), so all those symbols work.

It also means the shell interprets every character in the string. If any part comes from a user, a file name or a website, an attacker can slip in a command of their own. This is called **command injection**:

```python
name = "x; rm -rf ~"
subprocess.run(f"cat {name}", shell=True)   # also runs rm, deleting your files!
```

Prefer the list form, with no shell. You can usually do the shell's job in Python: `glob` for `*.txt`, `stdout=open(...)` for `>`, `env=` for settings, two `run` calls for `&&`.

If you truly need the shell, wrap every piece of outside text in `shlex.quote(value)`. It turns the text into a single harmless word for Linux and macOS shells.

`shlex.split("cmd 'two words' x")` splits a command string into a list the way those shells would, useful when a settings file stores commands as text. `shlex.join(list)` does the reverse, handy for printing what you ran.

`shlex` follows the rules of Linux and macOS shells; Windows quoting is different.
concepts.code:
import shlex, subprocess

evil = "notes.txt; echo INJECTED"
subprocess.run(f"echo cat {evil}", shell=True)
# cat notes.txt
# INJECTED                          <- second command ran

subprocess.run(f"echo cat {shlex.quote(evil)}", shell=True)
# cat notes.txt; echo INJECTED      <- one literal argument

subprocess.run(["echo", "cat", evil])  # list form: no shell, always safe
# cat notes.txt; echo INJECTED

args = shlex.split("grep -n 'two words' file.txt")
print(args)              # ['grep', '-n', 'two words', 'file.txt']
print(shlex.join(args))  # grep -n 'two words' file.txt
takeaways: shell=True runs a string through the shell, special symbols and all
Outside text in a shell string allows command injection
Prefer list arguments; if a shell is unavoidable, shlex.quote every outside value
pitfalls: Building shell strings with f-strings from text a user typed.

quiz.q: Which is safe for a user-supplied filename fn?
quiz.explain: The list form passes fn as one argument with no shell to interpret it.

concepts.name: Sending input and chaining commands
concepts.summary: Feed data to a command with input=, stop commands from waiting on the keyboard, and chain programs without a shell.
concepts.why: Many tools (sort, grep and others) read their input from standard input, and chaining commands is common in scripts.
concepts.body:
Besides its two outputs, a program has one input channel, **standard input** (stdin), normally the keyboard. `input=` sends data to the child's standard input and then closes it, so the program sees the end of the data, called **EOF** (end of file). Use a `str` with `text=True`, or `bytes` otherwise.

```python
r = subprocess.run(["sort"], input="b\na\n", capture_output=True, text=True)
```

If you don't pass `input` or `stdin`, the child reads from your standard input. A command that unexpectedly asks a question (a password, "Continue? [y/N]") then waits for a keyboard nobody is at, and your script hangs. In scripts that run unattended, such as scheduled jobs or servers, pass `stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL` so such reads see EOF immediately.

`stdin=` also accepts an open file, so `stdin=open("data.csv")` feeds a file to the program without loading it into memory.

To chain commands like the shell's `ps aux | grep python` (list running programs, keep the lines mentioning python) without `shell=True`, the simplest way is to pass the first command's output as the second one's input:

```python
ps = subprocess.run(["ps", "aux"], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
hits = subprocess.run(["grep", "python"], input=ps.stdout, capture_output=True, text=True)
```

This keeps the data in between in memory, which is fine for most outputs. For large amounts, connect the processes directly with `Popen` (a later lesson). Often the simplest chain is no chain at all: filter the output in Python.
concepts.code:
import subprocess, sys

r = subprocess.run(["sort", "-r"], input="apple\ncherry\nbanana\n",
                   capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
print(r.stdout.split())                   # ['cherry', 'banana', 'apple']

words = subprocess.run(["printf", "a b\nc\n"], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
count = subprocess.run(["wc", "-w"], input=words, capture_output=True, text=True)
print(count.stdout.strip())               # 3

r = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", "print(repr(input('name? ')))"],
                   stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, capture_output=True, text=True)
print(r.stderr.strip().splitlines()[-1])  # EOFError: EOF when reading a line
takeaways: input= writes data to stdin and closes it
stdin=DEVNULL prevents hangs on unexpected questions
Chain commands by passing one result's stdout as the next input
pitfalls: Letting a child read your standard input in a script that runs unattended, where a question then waits forever.

quiz.q: A script calls a tool that sometimes asks 'Continue? [y/N]'. How do you keep it from hanging?
quiz.explain: With DEVNULL the prompt reads EOF immediately instead of waiting on the terminal.

concepts.name: Timeouts
concepts.summary: Stop commands that run too long with timeout= and handle subprocess.TimeoutExpired.
concepts.why: A stuck download or build should not hang your script, or an automatic test run, forever.
concepts.body:
A **timeout** is a limit on how long you'll wait before giving up. `run(..., timeout=seconds)` waits at most that long. If the process is still running, `run` **kills** it, waits for it to end, and raises `subprocess.TimeoutExpired`. The exception has `cmd`, `timeout`, and whatever `output` / `stderr` was captured so far (bytes, even with `text=True`, and possibly `None`).

```python
try:
    subprocess.run(["curl", url], timeout=10, check=True)   # curl downloads a URL
except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
    print("curl took too long")
```

Notes:

- The timeout covers the whole run, including reading output.
- On Linux and macOS, the kill uses **SIGKILL**, the operating system's forceful "stop now" **signal** (a short message the system sends to a program). The child gets no chance to clean up. For a polite stop, use `Popen` and call `terminate()` first (a later lesson).
- With `shell=True`, only the shell is killed. Programs the shell started (the child's own children) may keep running and keep the output pipe open, so `run` can still hang after the timeout. Avoid the shell, or use a process group (an Expert lesson).

Choose timeouts generous enough for slow machines, and put the command and the timeout in the error message so failures are easy to understand.
concepts.code:
import subprocess, sys, time

t = time.perf_counter()
try:
    subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", "import time; print('start', flush=True); time.sleep(30)"],
                   timeout=0.5, capture_output=True, text=True)
except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as e:
    print(f"killed after {e.timeout}s")            # killed after 0.5s
    print("partial output:", e.output)             # partial output: b'start\n'
print(f"elapsed {time.perf_counter() - t:.1f}s")   # elapsed 0.5s
takeaways: timeout= kills the child and raises TimeoutExpired
Output captured so far is on the exception
Programs started by a shell may survive the kill
pitfalls: Expecting text output on TimeoutExpired; e.output is bytes even with text=True.

quiz.q: What does run(cmd, timeout=5) do when cmd is still running after 5 seconds?
options: Returns a result with returncode None
Raises TimeoutExpired and leaves the child running
Kills the child, waits for it, and raises TimeoutExpired
quiz.explain: run() kills the process and waits for it to end before raising.

concepts.name: Environment, working directory and PATH
concepts.summary: Control where a command runs and what environment it sees with cwd=, env= and shutil.which.
concepts.why: Build and deploy scripts need to run tools in a specific folder with specific settings.
concepts.body:
By default a child starts in your current **working directory** (the folder your script is "in") and gets a copy of your **environment variables**: named settings, like `PATH` or `HOME`, that every program receives when it starts.

`cwd=` runs the command in another folder without changing your own script's folder. It accepts a `str` or a `pathlib.Path`. **Relative paths** in the command (like `data.txt`, which don't start from the top of the disk) are then looked up from that folder.

`env=` **replaces** the child's environment variables entirely. Usually you want to add to them:

```python
env = {**os.environ, "NODE_ENV": "production"}       # your variables plus one more
subprocess.run(["npm", "run", "build"], env=env, cwd=project)   # build a web project
```

Passing only `{"NODE_ENV": "production"}` drops `PATH`, `HOME` and everything else, which breaks most programs. All keys and values must be strings.

Finding programs: the program is searched for on `PATH` (on Linux and macOS, the `PATH` in the `env` you pass). `shutil.which("ffmpeg")` returns the program's full path or `None`, letting you fail early with a helpful message. For Python itself, prefer `sys.executable`, so the child uses the same Python, with the same installed packages, as your script.

To run a module with that same Python, use `[sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", ...]`: the reliable way to call pip (Python's package installer) from code.
concepts.code:
import os, shutil, subprocess, sys, tempfile
from pathlib import Path

tmp = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(tmp / "data.txt").write_text("hi")

r = subprocess.run(["ls"], cwd=tmp, capture_output=True, text=True)
print(r.stdout.strip())                      # data.txt

env = {**os.environ, "GREETING": "hello"}
code = "import os; print(os.environ['GREETING'], 'PATH' in os.environ)"
r = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", code], env=env, capture_output=True, text=True)
print(r.stdout.strip())                      # hello True

print(shutil.which("sh"))                    # /usr/bin/sh (or /bin/sh)
print(shutil.which("no-such-tool"))          # None
takeaways: cwd= sets the child's working directory only
env= replaces the environment: merge with os.environ
shutil.which finds executables; sys.executable is the current Python
pitfalls: Passing env={'KEY': 'v'} alone, which removes PATH and breaks the command.

quiz.q: subprocess.run(['make'], env={'DEBUG': '1'}) fails with FileNotFoundError or odd errors. Why?
options: env replaces the whole environment, so PATH and others are gone
quiz.explain: env replaces everything, so PATH is gone; merge instead: env={**os.environ, 'DEBUG': '1'}.

concepts.name: Popen: streaming output
concepts.summary: Use subprocess.Popen to start a process without waiting and read its output line by line as it runs.
concepts.why: Long builds, servers and tools that keep printing need live output and control while they run.
concepts.body:
`run` waits for the program to finish. `Popen` starts the process and returns immediately, giving you an object to interact with it while it runs. It takes the same arguments as `run` (except `input`, `timeout`, `check` and `capture_output`).

```python
with subprocess.Popen(cmd, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True) as p:
    for line in p.stdout:
        print("got", line.rstrip())
print(p.returncode)
```

Key methods and attributes:

- `p.stdin`, `p.stdout`, `p.stderr`: file objects when you used `PIPE`.
- `p.poll()`: returns the exit code if finished, else `None`, without waiting.
- `p.wait(timeout=None)`: wait until it ends.
- `p.communicate(input, timeout)`: send input, read all output, wait.
- `p.pid` (its process ID), `p.returncode`, `p.terminate()`, `p.kill()`.

Use it as a **context manager**: on exit it closes the pipes and waits for the process, so you don't leave finished-but-never-waited-for processes behind (zombies, see the lesson on stopping processes).

Output buffering matters. Many programs collect their output in a **buffer** (a holding area) and write it in big chunks when the output goes to a pipe rather than a terminal, so lines arrive in bursts. For Python children, pass `-u` or set `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1`; other tools often have a `--line-buffered` flag.

In code that uses asyncio (Python's library for waiting on many things at once), use `asyncio.create_subprocess_exec` instead, which gives you streams you can `await`.
concepts.code:
import subprocess, sys, time

child = "import time\nfor i in range(3):\n    print('step', i, flush=True); time.sleep(0.2)"
t0 = time.perf_counter()
with subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, "-c", child],
                      stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True) as p:
    print("started pid", p.pid > 0, "poll:", p.poll())   # started pid True poll: None
    for line in p.stdout:                               # arrives live
        print(f"{time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f}s {line.rstrip()}")
print("exit code", p.returncode)
# 0.0s step 0
# 0.2s step 1
# 0.4s step 2
# exit code 0
takeaways: Popen starts a process without waiting and gives you live pipes
Iterate p.stdout for line-by-line streaming
Use Popen as a context manager so it is always waited for
pitfalls: Children that buffer their output when writing to a pipe, so 'live' lines only show up at the end.

quiz.q: What does p.poll() return while the child is still running?
options: It blocks until the child exits
quiz.explain: poll() never waits; it returns None until there is an exit code.

concepts.name: Pipes, communicate() and deadlocks
concepts.summary: Avoid hangs from full pipes with communicate(), and connect Popen processes into real pipelines.
concepts.why: The classic subprocess hang happens when parent and child both wait on a full pipe.
concepts.body:
A pipe has a small buffer (often 64 KiB). If a child writes more than that to a `PIPE` that nobody is reading, the child stops and waits. If the parent is meanwhile waiting too, say in `p.wait()` or while writing to the child's stdin, both wait forever. That's a **deadlock**: two sides each waiting for the other.

Typical traps:

- `p.wait()` with `stdout=PIPE` and lots of output,
- reading `p.stdout` to the end while the child is stuck writing to a full `stderr` pipe,
- writing a large input to `p.stdin` before reading any output.

`p.communicate(input=None, timeout=None)` solves this: it writes the input, reads stdout and stderr at the same time (using threads, or an operating-system call that watches several pipes at once), and waits. `run` uses it internally. If it times out, the process is not killed; call `p.kill()` and then `p.communicate()` again to collect the rest.

To build a real streaming pipeline, connect the processes' pipes to each other:

```python
p1 = Popen(["cat", "big.log"], stdout=PIPE)
p2 = Popen(["grep", "ERROR"], stdin=p1.stdout, stdout=PIPE)
p1.stdout.close()   # so p1 gets the SIGPIPE signal if p2 exits early
out, _ = p2.communicate()
```

Data flows directly from one child to the next without passing through Python.
concepts.code:
import subprocess, sys

big = "import sys; sys.stdout.write('x' * 1_000_000); sys.stderr.write('done')"
p = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, "-c", big],
                     stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE, text=True)
# p.wait() here could deadlock: 1 MB won't fit in the pipe buffer
out, err = p.communicate(timeout=10)
print(len(out), err, p.returncode)          # 1000000 done 0

gen = subprocess.Popen(["seq", "1", "100000"], stdout=subprocess.PIPE)
grep = subprocess.Popen(["grep", "-c", "7"], stdin=gen.stdout,
                        stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True)
gen.stdout.close()                          # let gen get SIGPIPE if grep exits
print(grep.communicate()[0].strip())        # 40951  (lines containing a 7)
gen.wait()
takeaways: A full, unread pipe makes the child wait; waiting on the child then makes you wait: deadlock
communicate() reads all pipes at the same time and waits safely
Connect Popen processes with stdin=p1.stdout for streaming pipelines
pitfalls: Calling p.wait() on a process whose stdout or stderr is a PIPE you haven't read.

quiz.q: Why does p.wait() sometimes hang forever when stdout=PIPE?
options: The child blocks writing to a full pipe that the parent isn't reading
The child never starts until communicate() is called
quiz.explain: The pipe buffer fills, the child waits for a reader, the parent waits for the child.

concepts.name: Stopping processes and exit statuses
concepts.summary: Stop processes gracefully with terminate() then kill(), and interpret negative return codes.
concepts.why: Tools that manage other programs, like test runners and development servers, must stop children cleanly and report why they ended.
concepts.body:
`p.terminate()` asks a process to stop. On Linux and macOS it sends **SIGTERM**, the polite "please stop" signal, which the program can catch to clean up first. `p.kill()` forces it with SIGKILL, which can't be caught. On Windows both call `TerminateProcess`. `p.send_signal(sig)` sends any signal, for example `signal.SIGINT` to imitate Ctrl+C.

The graceful pattern:

```python
p.terminate()
try:
    p.wait(timeout=5)
except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
    p.kill()
    p.wait()
```

Always `wait()` after stopping a process. Until a parent waits for it, a finished child stays in the operating system's list of processes as a **zombie**, an empty entry kept only so the parent can read its exit code.

On Linux and macOS, a **negative returncode** `-N` means the process was stopped by signal number N: `-15` is SIGTERM, `-9` is SIGKILL. A shell reports the same event as `128 + N`, so `137` from a shell or Docker means SIGKILL, often from Linux's out-of-memory killer, which stops programs when memory runs out. `signal.Signals(15).name` turns a number into `'SIGTERM'`.

`CalledProcessError`'s message also decodes this, saying "died with <Signals.SIGKILL: 9>".
concepts.code:
import signal, subprocess, sys

child = """
import signal, sys, time
signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, lambda *a: (print("child: cleaning up", flush=True), sys.exit(0)))
time.sleep(30)
"""
p = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, "-c", child])
try:
    p.wait(timeout=0.5)
except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
    p.terminate()                       # child: cleaning up
    print("graceful exit:", p.wait(timeout=5))      # graceful exit: 0

p = subprocess.Popen(["sleep", "30"])
p.kill()
code = p.wait()
print(code, signal.Signals(-code).name)            # -9 SIGKILL
takeaways: terminate() = SIGTERM (can be caught), kill() = SIGKILL
Always wait() after stopping a process
returncode -N means stopped by signal N; shells report 128+N
pitfalls: Calling kill() first, so the child never gets to finish writing files or release what it holds.

quiz.q: A child's returncode is -15 on Linux. What happened?
quiz.explain: A negative return code means the process was stopped by the signal with that number.

concepts.name: Process groups and killing trees
concepts.summary: Run children in their own process group or terminal session so you can signal or kill a whole process tree.
concepts.why: Shells, build tools and test runners start grandchildren that keep running if you only kill the direct child.
concepts.body:
Killing a process does not kill its children. If you start `sh -c "make && ./server"` and kill the shell on timeout, `make` or `server` keep running without a parent (orphans). If they hold the stdout pipe open, `communicate()` keeps waiting for them.

On Linux and macOS, put the child in its own **process group**, a set of processes that can be signalled together, and signal the whole group:

- `start_new_session=True` gives the child a new **terminal session** (the set of processes tied to one terminal) and a new process group, detached from your terminal.
- `process_group=0` (3.11+) only creates a new process group, keeping the session.

Then `os.killpg(p.pid, signal.SIGTERM)` (the group's ID is its first process's ID) reaches every process in the group, including grandchildren, unless they deliberately moved to another group.

Side effect: a child in a new session no longer receives Ctrl+C from your terminal, so pass signals on yourself if you need that.

On Windows, use `creationflags=subprocess.CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP` and send `CTRL_BREAK_EVENT`, or use Job Objects (through third-party libraries) to kill a whole tree.

The third-party `psutil` library can also list `children(recursive=True)` and kill each one, a fallback that works on every system.
concepts.code:
import os, signal, subprocess, time

# The shell starts a grandchild (sleep) that outlives a plain kill.
cmd = "sleep 30 & echo grandchild $!; wait"
p = subprocess.Popen(["sh", "-c", cmd], stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True,
                     start_new_session=True)
gpid = int(p.stdout.readline().split()[1])
print(os.getpgid(gpid) == p.pid)     # True: same group as the shell

os.killpg(p.pid, signal.SIGTERM)     # signal the whole group
p.wait()
t = time.perf_counter()
print(repr(p.stdout.read()))         # '' -> EOF: no process holds the pipe
print(f"{time.perf_counter() - t:.1f}s")  # 0.0s (p.kill() alone: blocks ~30s)
p.stdout.close()
takeaways: Killing a process leaves its children running
start_new_session=True or process_group=0 puts the child in its own group
os.killpg(pid, sig) signals the whole tree
pitfalls: Using shell=True with timeout and expecting the timeout to stop everything the shell started.

quiz.q: Why doesn't run('sh -c "server"', shell=True, timeout=5) always stop the server?
options: Only the shell is killed; the server is a separate grandchild process
quiz.explain: Signals go to one pid; put the tree in a process group and use killpg.

concepts.name: File descriptors and secure spawning
concepts.summary: Control which open files and connections children inherit, and run them with fewer rights, using close_fds, pass_fds, user and umask.
concepts.why: Children that hold on to the parent's open files, or run with more rights than they need, cause subtle security and reliability bugs.
concepts.body:
Every open file, pipe end or network connection a program has is identified by a **file descriptor**, a small number the operating system hands out. When a child starts, it may inherit open descriptors from the parent. Such leaks cause real bugs: a child holding your server's listening network connection keeps the port busy after the server restarts, and a child holding a pipe's write end means the reader never sees EOF.

Python's defaults are safe. Descriptors created by Python are **non-inheritable** (PEP 446), and `close_fds=True` (the default) closes everything in the child except 0, 1 and 2 (standard input, output and error). To deliberately hand over specific descriptors, list them in `pass_fds=(fd,)`.

Other Linux and macOS controls on `Popen` and `run`:

- `user=`, `group=`, `extra_groups=` (3.9+): when your script runs as root, the all-powerful administrator, run the child as a less powerful user.
- `umask=` (3.9+): which permissions files created by the child will lack.
- `preexec_fn=`: runs Python code in the child just before it turns into the new program. Avoid it: it isn't safe in programs that use threads. Use the dedicated parameters (`start_new_session`, `process_group`, `user`) instead.
- `executable=`: run a different program file than `args[0]`; `args[0]` then becomes the name the program sees for itself.

Security checklist: list arguments (no shell), full paths for sensitive tools, a minimal `env`, no secrets in arguments (anyone can see them by listing running programs with `ps`), and `stdin=DEVNULL`.
concepts.code:
import os, subprocess, sys

r, w = os.pipe()
print(os.get_inheritable(w))                  # False (PEP 446)

child = "import os, sys; fd = int(sys.argv[1]); os.write(fd, b'via fd'); os.close(fd)"
subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", child, str(w)], pass_fds=(w,), check=True)
os.close(w)
print(os.read(r, 100))                        # b'via fd'

res = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", child, str(r)],
                     capture_output=True, text=True)
print(res.stderr.strip().splitlines()[-1])    # OSError: [Errno 9] Bad file descriptor
os.close(r)
takeaways: Python-created descriptors aren't inherited, and close_fds=True is the default
pass_fds hands specific descriptors to the child
Prefer user=, umask= and start_new_session over preexec_fn
pitfalls: Passing secrets on the command line, where any user can read them with ps.

options: It runs after the new program starts, so it has no effect
It can deadlock in programs that use threads
quiz.explain: Running Python code in the child before the new program starts is unsafe with threads; the dedicated parameters avoid it.

concepts.name: How processes are spawned
concepts.summary: See how subprocess creates processes: fork and exec, vfork and posix_spawn on Linux and macOS, CreateProcess on Windows.
concepts.why: How processes are started explains speed at scale, memory errors in big programs, and Windows quoting bugs.
concepts.body:
On Linux and macOS, the classic way to start a program is **fork** (copy the current process) then **exec** (replace the copy with the new program). subprocess does this in C (`_posixsubprocess`), doing the minimal setup in between: connect the pipes, change folder, set the session, drop rights.

Forking a large process used to be slow, and could fail with an out-of-memory error (`ENOMEM`) on systems that refuse to promise more memory than they have. That happened even though the copy shares the parent's memory until one side changes it (**copy-on-write**). So CPython picks faster methods when it can:

- **posix_spawn** on Linux and macOS, when the arguments allow it (for example `close_fds=False` and no `cwd`, `preexec_fn` or session options),
- **vfork** on Linux (3.10+), which borrows the parent's memory until exec instead of copying its memory bookkeeping; used whenever it is safe.

Exec failures (a missing program, a bad `cwd`) are reported back to the parent through a dedicated pipe and raised there as `FileNotFoundError` and similar, which is why you get a proper exception rather than exit code 127.

On Windows, `CreateProcess` takes a **single command-line string**. subprocess converts your list with `list2cmdline`, following Microsoft's usual quoting rules; programs that read their command line differently (notably `cmd.exe`) may see different arguments.
concepts.code:
import subprocess, sys, time

print(subprocess.list2cmdline(["prog", "a b", 'say "hi"']))
# prog "a b" "say \"hi\""   (Windows quoting rules)

N = 50
t = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(N):
    subprocess.run(["true"])
print(f"{(time.perf_counter() - t) / N * 1000:.2f} ms per spawn")  # ~1 ms

try:
    subprocess.run(["true"], cwd="/no/such/dir")
except FileNotFoundError as e:
    print("raised in parent:", e.strerror)   # raised in parent: No such file or directory
takeaways: On Linux and macOS, starting a program is fork/vfork + exec, or posix_spawn when options allow
Exec errors come back through a pipe and are raised in the parent
Windows gets one command-line string built by list2cmdline
pitfalls: Assuming Windows programs receive your list elements exactly; quoting depends on how the target parses its command line.

quiz.q: How does subprocess raise FileNotFoundError for a missing program on POSIX, when the error happens in the child after fork?
options: The child reports the exec error to the parent through a dedicated pipe
It parses the shell's error message
It checks PATH before forking and never forks
The kernel raises it directly in Python
quiz.explain: The child writes the error number to a dedicated pipe, which the parent reads and turns into an exception.
